title: Stopping, standing and parking
summary: When you may stop, stand or park, when it is completely forbidden, and how to do it correctly and safely.

lessons.title: Stopping, standing and parking: the legal difference
lessons.summary: Three actions that look similar, but the law treats them differently — and the difference decides which signs apply and when there is an offence.
lessons.body:
"I only stopped for a second" is one of the most common things drivers say to a police officer writing a parking ticket — and it usually does not help, because the law has its own definition of what actually happened. [[term:stopping|Stopping]], [[term:standing|standing]] and [[term:parking|parking]] are three legally different actions, and the difference between them decides which signs apply and when there is an offence.

# The legal definition
The law explicitly defines only parking:

:::law
**Parking** is leaving the vehicle standing for any length of time — even a few seconds — when this is not done to pick up or set down passengers, or to load or unload goods, immediately and without a break. Even a vehicle with a driver inside and the engine running can count as parked, if it is not standing only for that purpose (the Traffic Regulations, regulation 1).
:::

From this definition you can derive the other two. If the stop is **only** to pick up or set down a passenger, or to load or unload goods, continuously and without a break — that is [[term:standing|standing]], not parking. The moment there is a break in the middle, or the reason is different, it is already parking.

[[term:stopping|Stopping]] is shorter still: a break in the journey where the driver does not really "leave" the vehicle, but waits to move on immediately — at a red light, at a [[sign:302|Stop]] sign, to give way, or even in a traffic jam. Regulations 69, 71 and 72 always mention the three actions together ("a person shall not stop a vehicle, shall not stand it, shall not park it"), without defining stopping and standing separately — but this consistent wording is what makes the difference clear.

# Summary table
| | How long it lasts | What it is for | Is the driver ready to move on immediately |
|---|---|---|---|
| Stopping | Shortest | Traffic, a light, a sign, giving way | Yes |
| Standing | Short and continuous | Picking up/setting down passengers, immediate loading/unloading | Usually yes |
| Parking | Any length of time | Any other purpose | Not necessarily |

# Why it matters in practice
This difference is not theoretical: it is written right on the signs. Sign [[sign:432]] prohibits **parking** only — a short stop, loading and unloading, and picking up or setting down passengers are still allowed there. Sign [[sign:433]] prohibits **everything**: you cannot stop there even for a moment, unless it is needed to avoid an accident or to comply with another requirement in the regulations.

:::tip
When a sign permits stopping, standing or parking, it overrides the general prohibitions in the regulations (regulation 76(a)). That is why you can sometimes see a local sign that allows parking in exactly the spot that looks forbidden.
:::

Even a stop or a period of standing that happens somewhere "allowed" can still be forbidden if it actually causes a problem: you must not leave a vehicle standing in a way that obstructs the free flow of traffic, or that hides a sign from other road users (regulation 71). In other words, even without being on the list of forbidden places, a vehicle that blocks a lane or hides a sign is still committing an offence.

Stopping or parking in a forbidden place is a parking offence just the same, and can bring a fine even without "really parking" — for example {{fine:parking-general-prohibited-sign}} for stopping or parking where a sign forbids it.

:::example
A driver who stops for a moment by a bus stop to let a passenger out and drives off immediately — that is permitted standing. The same driver who turns off the engine and goes to buy a coffee for two minutes — that is already parking, and it is forbidden at a bus stop. A taxi driver who stops where there is no stopping sign to let a passenger out, and at that moment blocks a "Stop" sign from another driver's view with the body of the vehicle, is also committing an offence — even though the stop itself was short and apparently lawful.
:::
keyPoints: Parking is defined by law as leaving the vehicle standing for any length of time, other than to immediately pick up/set down passengers or immediately load/unload goods (reg. 1).
Standing is a short, continuous stop for exactly that purpose; stopping is a temporary break in the journey where the driver waits to move on immediately.
Sign [[sign:432|432]] prohibits parking only; sign [[sign:433|433]] prohibits stopping and standing too.
A sign that permits stopping, standing or parking overrides the general prohibition in the regulations.
Even in a permitted spot, a stop that obstructs traffic or hides a sign is forbidden (reg. 71).

lessons.title: Where you may not stop, stand or park
lessons.summary: The list of places where the law forbids stopping, standing and parking — with the exact distances.
lessons.body:
Regulation 72 lists a long series of places where you may not stop, stand or park a vehicle — all of it or part of it — except to avoid an accident, to comply with another requirement in the regulations, or if a sign permits otherwise.

# Fixed distances set by law
Some of the prohibitions are set by an exact distance from a particular point:

| Where from | The forbidden distance |
|---|---|
| From a junction (inside it and around it) | {{fact:park.no_stop.junction_m}} |
| Before a pedestrian crossing | {{fact:park.no_stop.pedestrian_crossing_m}} |
| Before a stop line | {{fact:park.no_stop.stop_line_m}} |
| Before and after a railway level crossing | {{fact:park.no_stop.railway_crossing_m}} |
| On a bridge, in a tunnel, and before and after them | {{fact:park.no_stop.bridge_tunnel_m}} |
| Before and after a "bus stop" sign (with no other marking) | {{fact:park.no_stop.bus_stop_m}} |
| Before and after a single taxi-stopping-point sign | {{fact:park.no_stop.taxi_stand_single_m}} |
| Before and after a soldier-transport stop | {{fact:park.no_stop.soldier_transport_m}} |
| Before and after a local train station sign | {{fact:park.no_stop.train_station_platform_m}} |

:::remember
Beside a bus stop, you may stop or park on the opposite side of the road, if the road there is at least 12 metres wide.
:::

# Prohibitions without a numeric distance
Other places are forbidden entirely, regardless of distance: on the left side of the road (except on a one-way road), on the [[term:sidewalk|pavement]] (other than a place set aside for that), on a marked cycle path (unless it does not obstruct anyone), at the entrance to an area meant for vehicles, right next to another vehicle that is already standing or parked, beside a [[term:traffic-island|traffic island]] or a pedestrian safety barrier, in a single lane with a continuous dividing line, in a public-transport lane and within the bus stop itself, and on a road with a [[sign:401|Road closed]] sign ahead of it — if you cannot enter there at all, you obviously cannot stop there either.

A large bus has its own stricter rule: a bus designed to carry twenty passengers or more may not stand or park on the road — even where another vehicle is allowed to — unless a sign says otherwise (regulation 72(b)).

# Signs and kerb colours
Sign [[sign:432]] prohibits parking only; [[sign:433]] prohibits everything; [[sign:434]] marks the end of the section they apply to. [[sign:435]] and [[sign:436]] prohibit parking by a heavy goods vehicle over 10,000 kg in a particular area. [[sign:437]] reserves a spot for a vehicle with a disabled badge only.

The colour of the kerb adds information: red-and-white forbids all stopping and parking; alternating blue permits paid parking; red-and-yellow permits stopping only for the stated type of vehicle, for pick-up and drop-off only. A black-and-white kerb is just a highly visible marking — it **does not** forbid parking, despite a common misconception.

:::note Increased-fine zone
In certain places — for example near schools or in busy sections — an order can designate an "increased-fine zone", marked with a special sign reading "increased fine". Forbidden parking or stopping in such a zone brings a higher-than-usual fine, even though the reason for the prohibition itself is the same as in any other forbidden place.
:::

:::fine
Stopping or parking where a sign forbids it: {{fine:parking-general-prohibited-sign}}. Parking on the pavement: {{fine:parking-sidewalk}}. Parking in a forbidden spot next to a disabled parking space in a way that blocks it: {{fine:parking-disabled-space-obstruct}}.
:::
keyPoints: Regulation 72 forbids stopping, standing and parking in certain places — except to avoid an accident or if a sign permits otherwise.

Fixed distances: {{fact:park.no_stop.junction_m}} from a junction, a pedestrian crossing and a stop line; {{fact:park.no_stop.railway_crossing_m}} from a level crossing; {{fact:park.no_stop.bridge_tunnel_m}} from a bridge and a tunnel; {{fact:park.no_stop.bus_stop_m}} from a bus stop.
Blanket prohibitions: the left side, the pavement, a marked cycle path, next to another vehicle, a single lane with a continuous line; a bus with 20 passengers or more may not stand almost anywhere.
A red-and-white kerb forbids everything; blue permits paid parking; red-and-yellow permits stopping only for a permitted vehicle; black-and-white is just a marking.

lessons.title: Parking correctly: parallel, angled and on a slope
lessons.summary: The permitted distance from the kerb, how to stop on a slope, and how to get out of the vehicle without endangering anyone.
lessons.body:
Parking correctly is not just "not blocking" — it has precise rules, designed to keep space free for other vehicles and to keep everyone who gets out of the vehicle safe.

# Parallel parking
In [[term:parallel-parking|parallel parking]], you position the vehicle in a line parallel to the edge of the road, with the wheels nearest the kerb no more than {{fact:park.curb_distance_max}} from it — whether or not there is a kerb (regulation 75). This small distance is not arbitrary: it leaves other vehicles as much free lane width as possible, and does not block a cycle path or the space needed to open a door on the other side.

Angled or perpendicular parking is allowed only where the local signage authority has permitted it and marked it explicitly — without that marking, the default is always parallel parking.

[[fig:sp-parallel-parking]]

# Parking on a slope
On a slope, you must chock the wheels correctly before getting out of the vehicle (regulation 74(c)):
- **Going downhill**: turn the front wheels toward the kerb or the edge of the road, and engage reverse gear — so that if the vehicle moves, the kerb will stop it.
- **Going uphill**: turn the front wheels away from the kerb, toward the road (or toward the edge of the road if there is no kerb), and engage forward gear.
- In an automatic vehicle, engage park gear (P), which is made exactly for this situation.
- If the manufacturer has set different instructions for parking on a slope, follow the manufacturer's instructions, which override the general rule.

A vehicle that is required to carry safety chocks (portable wheel chocks) and that stops or is parked on a sloped road — the driver must also place them under the rear wheels, as extra backup for the parking brake. Which vehicles must carry safety chocks, and more detail on braking systems in heavy vehicles, is in the [[chapter:heavy-vehicles|heavy vehicles]] chapter.

# Leaving the vehicle safely
Before getting out, make sure the vehicle cannot move: turn off the engine, remove the ignition key (if there is one), and apply [[term:parking-brake|the parking brake]] (regulation 74). An unattended vehicle always needs both safeguards — the engine off and [[term:parking-brake|the parking brake]] applied, not just one of them.

# Getting out of the vehicle safely
Before opening a door — look back. You must not open a door without taking every precaution to keep road users safe, and you must not open a door while the vehicle is moving (regulation 80). Get in and out of the vehicle only while it is standing, and from the side facing the edge of the road where it is lawfully parked — a passenger sitting beside the driver may also get out from the other side, after taking care (regulation 81).

:::danger The door trap
A cyclist or motorcyclist passing a parked vehicle cannot always stop in time if a door suddenly opens. This is the most important reason to look back before opening any door — especially for [[term:vulnerable-road-user|vulnerable road users]].
:::
keyPoints: In parallel parking: the wheels nearest the kerb no more than {{fact:park.curb_distance_max}} from it (reg. 75).
Downhill: front wheels toward the kerb, reverse gear. Uphill: front wheels toward the road, forward gear (reg. 74).
Before getting out of the vehicle: engine off, key removed, parking brake applied.
Before opening a door, look back — you must not open a door while the vehicle is moving, and not without taking care (reg. 80).

lessons.title: Special parking: disabled, paid, and at night outside town
lessons.summary: When parking is reserved, when you pay, and what is different when the vehicle stands at night outside a town.
lessons.body:
Not all parking spaces are equal. Some are reserved, some are paid, and some call for extra care when it happens at night outside a town.

# Disabled parking
Sign [[sign:437]] reserves a parking spot exclusively for a vehicle carrying a valid [[term:disabled-person|disabled]] badge, while the vehicle is actually being used by the person the badge was issued to — not just any vehicle that happens to be carrying a disabled person, but one that actually serves them. Sometimes a [[sign:439]] sign with specific vehicle details is placed underneath it — then the spot is reserved for that vehicle alone. Blocking a disabled person's vehicle that is lawfully parked in its reserved spot: {{fine:parking-disabled-blocking}}. Parking in a forbidden spot nearby that stops a disabled person getting into or out of their vehicle: {{fine:parking-disabled-space-obstruct}}.

# Paid parking
A kerb painted with alternating blue marks parking that is allowed for payment, under sign 439 placed next to sign 626 or 627 (which give the tariff and the hours). You must pay by the means specified — a machine, an app or a card — and keep to the payment hours and the maximum parking time if one is set. A blue kerb with no tariff sign beside it is not enough to know that the parking is paid — look for the accompanying sign. Outside the payment hours stated on the sign, that same spot can be completely free — it is the clock that decides, not just the colour of the kerb.

# Loading and unloading spots
A kerb painted red-and-yellow permits stopping only for the type of vehicle stated on the sign above it, and only for picking up and setting down passengers or for loading and unloading — not for parking. A spot like this is usually meant for public transport or taxis.

# Parking on an expressway
On an expressway, picking up or setting down passengers, and also stopping, standing or parking a vehicle anywhere between the boundaries of the road, are completely forbidden — unless marked otherwise (regulation 69(c)). This is why even a breakdown on an expressway calls for special care: there is no "ordinary shoulder" to stop on like on a normal road, only a narrower dedicated shoulder meant mainly for breakdowns, not for stopping by choice — for example to answer the phone or check a map.

# Parking at night outside a town
On a non-urban road marked as a main or regional road, it is almost always forbidden to stand or park a vehicle on the carriageway or on the shoulder, attended or not. It is allowed only in defined cases (regulation 69(b)):
- picking up or setting down passengers on the shoulder
- rescuing casualties, or a vehicle that has broken down
- public works, when there is no other way to carry them out
- an IDF vehicle that has stopped to carry out a military task

If the vehicle does stand outside town during lighting-up time anyway, a works vehicle, a bus, or a goods vehicle over {{fact:equip.hazard_lights_heavy}} must show a flashing amber lamp or all the hazard lights (regulation 70(b)) — the full procedure for a breakdown is set out in [[lesson:sp-roadside|Stopping outside town for a breakdown]].
keyPoints: Sign [[sign:437|437]] reserves parking for a vehicle with a valid disabled badge; blocking it and blocking a disabled person getting in or out are separate offences.
Alternating blue kerb = paid parking under sign 439 plus 626/627.
Red-and-yellow kerb = stopping only, for the permitted type of vehicle, for pick-up/drop-off or loading/unloading.
On an expressway, all stopping, standing and parking is completely forbidden — unless marked otherwise (reg. 69(c)).
On a non-urban road marked as main or regional, stopping, standing and parking are forbidden almost always — except in cases defined by law.

lessons.title: Breakdown on the road: how to stop safely outside town
lessons.summary: Your vehicle has broken down outside town: where to move it, what lights to turn on, and how to mark that it is standing.
lessons.body:
A breakdown outside town is one of the most dangerous moments in driving: your vehicle is standing still, and other vehicles are approaching it at full speed. Getting the order of actions right decides everything.

# Moving the vehicle off the road
When the vehicle breaks down while driving and is forced to stand on the road, the driver must do everything necessary to move it to the shoulder and get it clear of the road as quickly as possible (regulation 69(e)). Stop as far from the lane as you can, beyond the safety barrier if there is one, and turn on the hazard lights the moment you start to stop — even before you put out the triangle. The hazard lights are the first and fastest signal that other vehicles get.

# Marking that the vehicle is standing
For a vehicle forced to stand on the road, the driver must place a [[term:warning-triangle|warning triangle]] so that it can be seen by a vehicle approaching from behind from at least {{fact:equip.triangle.visibility}} away (regulation 70(a)). Before a bend or the crest of a hill that hides the vehicle, place the triangle further back, to give approaching vehicles real reaction time. If the vehicle stands outside town during lighting-up time, a bus, a works vehicle, or a goods vehicle over {{fact:equip.hazard_lights_heavy}} must also show a flashing amber lamp, or all the direction indicators together (regulation 70(b)).

:::tech Portable warning lamp
In a vehicle whose permitted gross weight exceeds 3,500 kg, the flashing amber lamp must be visible from at least {{fact:equip.warning_lamp.visibility}} away, and must keep working continuously for {{fact:equip.warning_lamp.hours}}, independently of the vehicle's battery.
:::

# Getting out of the vehicle safely
A [[term:high-vis-vest|high-visibility vest]] must be carried in every motor vehicle (except a motorcycle). Anyone who gets out of the vehicle on a non-urban road must wear it — this duty applies by day and by night alike, unless a passenger who has already got out is wearing a vest first. Get out on the safe side (away from the traffic), not the side facing the road.

# Repairing on the spot, or not
You may repair a minor fault that delays starting or continuing the journey on the spot where it happened, provided the repair does not cause a nuisance to road users, and the vehicle does not stay there more than 24 hours (regulation 154). You must not repair a vehicle on the carriageway itself, or use a public parking spot for a general repair — only for a fault that occurred while driving. Anyone repairing or changing a wheel must not stand with their body projecting beyond the side of the vehicle toward the flow of traffic, unless there really is no other way.

# Where to stop and wait
Beyond the shoulder and the safety barrier, and not on a section with a bend or the crest of a hill that hides you from approaching vehicles. Wait well away from the road and from the vehicle itself, not beside it on the traffic side — a vehicle that hits the stranded vehicle could also hit anyone standing next to it.
keyPoints: Breakdown while driving: move the vehicle to the shoulder and get it clear of the road as fast as possible (reg. 69(e)), and turn on the hazard lights at once.

The warning triangle is visible from at least {{fact:equip.triangle.visibility}} away (reg. 70(a)); a heavy vehicle outside town during lighting-up time must also show a flashing lamp or hazard lights.
A high-visibility vest is required every time you get out of the vehicle on a non-urban road, by day and by night.
A minor repair is allowed only where the fault occurred, without causing a nuisance, and for no more than 24 hours (reg. 154).
Stop and stand well away from the road and the flow of traffic — not between the vehicle and passing traffic.
